slides.title: A reporter gene makes a selected cellular process visible
body: A **reporter gene** encodes a product that researchers can detect, such as a fluorescent protein. Delivering the gene allows selected cells to manufacture the reporter themselves. A stable fluorescent label reveals cell position and shape, whereas a responsive reporter changes its signal when a particular cellular variable, such as calcium concentration, changes.

Gene delivery and gene editing perform different operations. A viral vector can introduce an additional reporter without deliberately cutting a selected genomic sequence. **Gene editing** changes a specified DNA target within the cell's genome. The fluorescent cells in an imaging experiment therefore do not automatically indicate that an endogenous gene was removed or repaired in those cells.

In calcium imaging, the expressed protein combines molecular recognition with light emission. Calcium binding changes the reporter's fluorescence, and a camera converts the emitted photons into image values. The CaImAn source recording visualizes activity extracted from labeled zebrafish brain tissue, illustrating how genetically introduced reporters provide optical access to neuronal populations throughout a recorded volume of nervous tissue.

slides.title: Antisense molecules change how a selected RNA is used
body: An **antisense oligonucleotide**, or **ASO**, is a short synthetic strand designed to bind a complementary RNA sequence. Complementary bases pair, allowing the ASO to recognize a selected transcript among many RNA molecules. Once bound, an ASO can alter the RNA's processing or availability, changing how much functional protein is produced from that transcript inside the targeted cells.

Some ASOs recruit enzymes that degrade the bound RNA. Others alter **splicing**, the process that removes selected RNA segments before the mature message is translated. Changing splicing can restore a useful protein sequence or reduce an unwanted product, depending on the RNA target and where the ASO binds relative to the sequences controlling RNA processing.

An ASO acts at the RNA level rather than necessarily changing the underlying DNA sequence. Its effect therefore depends on delivery to the relevant cells, binding to the transcript, and the time required for existing proteins to turn over. A rapid change in RNA abundance can precede a slower change in cellular physiology when the original protein remains functional for some time.

slides.title: Spatial RNA measurements locate molecular cell types
body: Yao and colleagues combined RNA sequencing with **MERFISH**, a method that detects selected RNA molecules at their original locations in tissue. Fluorescent probes bind complementary RNA sequences. Successive rounds of imaging assign a pattern of detected signals to each molecular target, allowing many genes to be measured while preserving the positions of the cells within the brain section.

The measured transcripts formed molecular profiles that could be compared with the sequencing-based cell groups. A cell's spatial location was therefore paired with an expression-based identity. This allowed the investigators to determine where particular populations occurred, including mixtures of molecularly distinct cells within a single anatomical region that would appear more uniform in an image showing only cell-body shape or tissue boundaries.

The resulting maps revealed region-specific organization of neuronal and non-neuronal populations. Some expression-defined populations were restricted to particular territories, while related populations occupied broader areas. Retaining the spatial coordinates made it possible to examine boundaries and neighboring cell types, rather than inferring anatomical position from a detached cell's RNA profile after it had been removed from the surrounding tissue for sequencing.

slides.title: A connectome traces sensory inputs to brain outputs
body: Dorkenwald and colleagues grouped reconstructed fly neurons according to their position and direction of information flow. **Afferent neurons** bring signals into the brain from sensory organs or other regions, while **efferent neurons** carry signals outward. Intrinsic neurons remain within the brain, where their branches provide intermediate processing between incoming sensory pathways and outgoing commands to other parts of the animal.

The reconstruction distinguished populations reaching the ventral nerve cord, the insect structure containing many motor circuits. Descending neurons carry signals from the brain toward these circuits, while ascending neurons bring information in the opposite direction. The labeled source renderings preserve these anatomical categories, allowing students to recognize how neurons with different projection patterns occupy the same connected nervous system.

The researchers traced synaptic pathways from selected visual inputs toward descending outputs. Each step followed identified connections in the reconstructed specimen rather than proximity alone between two visible branches. This established candidate anatomical routes through which visual information could influence movement, with intermediate neurons contributing additional processing before signals reached populations projecting out of the brain toward the nerve cord.

slides.title: CRISPR directs molecular tools to a chosen DNA sequence
body: **CRISPR–Cas systems** use a guide RNA to direct a protein to a complementary DNA sequence near a suitable recognition motif. In common editing approaches, **Cas9** cuts the DNA at that location. The cell then repairs the break, and the repair process can change the sequence, interrupt a gene, or incorporate a supplied change under appropriate conditions in the targeted cells.

slides.title: Regulatory gene combinations distinguish cell identities
body: A **transcription factor** is a protein that binds DNA and influences the expression of other genes. Yao and colleagues examined these regulators across the mouse brain cell atlas. Their analysis found combinations of transcription-factor expression that distinguished molecular populations, providing a description of cellular identity based on a coordinated gene-expression pattern rather than one isolated marker in a single brain region.

Cells with related functions can share some expressed genes while differing in others. Comparing combinations makes it possible to separate populations that would be merged by a broad marker such as a transmitter-synthesis enzyme. The atlas organized these differences at several nested levels, preserving both general identities and narrower cell groups with more specific expression profiles across the brain.

These profiles can guide the design of future targeting strategies. A researcher seeking one population can examine which regulatory or marker genes distinguish it from neighboring cells. The atlas identifies candidates for this targeting; an experimental delivery system must still be tested to establish where the reporter or manipulator is actually expressed before its physiological effect is assigned to the intended population.

slides.title: Homecage tracking follows naturally occurring behavior
body: Tang and colleagues tested ADPT on mice interacting in a homecage setting. The camera observed actions occurring over time rather than only movements triggered by a brief laboratory cue. Tracking body parts and identities across these recordings allowed positions from different individuals to be distinguished even as the animals moved close together or changed their orientation relative to the camera.

The researchers compared predicted locations with annotated positions and examined performance across individuals. A method that works in a sparse arena can encounter new visual problems in a cage containing several bodies and background objects. Their homecage evaluation therefore tested whether the same tracking approach could preserve landmark placement under a different combination of scene complexity and social interaction.

Continuous positional data can describe when an animal approaches another, remains still, or moves between parts of the cage. Aligning those events with a neural recording requires shared timing between the camera and recording system. An event timestamp can then identify the corresponding electrical or optical samples, allowing naturally occurring actions to be examined without assuming that all behavior begins at an experimenter's cue.

slides.title: A decoder turns neural signals into device commands
body: A **brain–computer interface**, or **BCI**, uses measured neural activity to operate an external device. A recording system captures electrical or optical signals, and a **decoder** converts patterns in those measurements into an output. The output might specify cursor velocity, a selected letter, or a stimulation command delivered to a second part of the nervous system.

The decoder is calibrated using examples that pair a neural pattern with a known action or intention-related task. During later use, it receives a new pattern and estimates the appropriate output. A cursor controller might map the population's current activity onto horizontal and vertical motion, allowing the user to influence the cursor by changing the recorded neural pattern over time.

The person sees the cursor move and can adjust their next attempt. This feedback completes a **closed loop** between neural activity, decoder output, visible device behavior, and subsequent neural activity. The recording electrodes do not need to activate a muscle directly because the external computer receives the command that would otherwise have contributed to an action through the body's motor pathways.

slides.title: Attempted speech retains distinct motor-cortex patterns
body: Willett and colleagues implanted microelectrode arrays in a participant with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or **ALS**, whose speech had become unintelligible. The arrays recorded activity in cortical regions involved in speech production. The participant attempted spoken sounds and words while the researchers measured how the recorded neuronal population changed across different movements of the mouth and different attempted speech items.

Producing speech normally requires coordinated movements of the lips, tongue, jaw, and larynx. Cortical populations contribute patterns related to these **articulators**, the structures shaping the speech sound. In this participant, patterns distinguishing attempted articulatory actions remained detectable despite the severe impairment of intelligible vocal output, allowing the experiment to access the cortical activity preceding an unsuccessful spoken response.

The recorded patterns were distributed across many electrodes, with different sounds and movements producing different population responses. A decoder could use these differences rather than requiring a separate electrode for every word. The experiment therefore supplied a neural input that retained information about attempted speech even when listening to the participant's natural vocalizations did not provide an intelligible version of the intended sentence.

slides.title: A speech decoder estimates successive sound units
body: The speech decoder first converted electrode signals into measurements such as threshold-crossing counts and spike-band power. A **threshold crossing** marks an electrical event that exceeds a selected detection level. These measurements summarized the activity available from the implanted arrays during successive short intervals while the participant attempted to speak sentences displayed on the screen.

A recurrent neural network then estimated a sequence of **phonemes**, the sound units that distinguish words in a language. A language model used those estimates to identify likely word sequences. The neural model therefore supplied information about the attempted sound pattern, while the language model supplied constraints about plausible combinations of sounds and words in the final decoded sentence.

In the real-time demonstration, the participant prepared a sentence, attempted to speak when cued, and viewed the decoder's output. The system then read the resulting text aloud using synthetic speech. The study reported attempted-speech decoding at 62 words per minute, a measurement of the interface's output during this task rather than a restoration of normal vocal movement through the participant's speech muscles.

slides.title: Related speech sounds evoke related cortical patterns
body: Willett and colleagues compared the neural responses to different speech sounds with measurements of articulatory movements. Sounds produced using similar mouth configurations tended to evoke related population patterns. This organization suggests that the recorded cortical activity retained aspects of the motor structure of speech rather than representing each attempted sound as a completely independent signal unrelated to the others in the participant's neural population.

A **phoneme representation** describes how the activity pattern differs across speech sounds. Comparing patterns can reveal whether lip-related sounds, tongue-related sounds, or other articulatory groups occupy nearby positions in a mathematical representation of the data. These positions summarize measured similarities; they do not correspond to literal locations of the sounds inside a small physical map of cortex.

The preservation of this articulatory structure helps explain why a decoder trained on sound components can generate many word sequences. The system does not need a separately recorded cortical pattern for every possible sentence. It combines information about the changing attempted sounds with a language model, allowing the same underlying sound distinctions to contribute to different words and phrases during communication through the interface.

body: The speech study also tested a condition in which the participant silently mouthed the words rather than attempting to produce vocalizations. slides.title: A brain–spine interface bridges an injured pathway
body: Lorach and colleagues developed a **brain–spine interface** for a participant with a chronic spinal cord injury. Cortical implants recorded signals over regions involved in controlling the legs. A processor decoded these signals and adjusted electrical stimulation delivered below the injury, providing a digital route between attempted movement in the brain and spinal circuits that could help activate the legs.

The cortical recording system used **electrocorticography**, or **ECoG**, which measures population electrical activity from electrodes positioned near the cortical surface. This differs from the penetrating microelectrode arrays used in the speech study. The interface decoded features of these surface signals associated with attempted leg actions, then translated the estimated action into a spinal stimulation program matched to that movement.

An implanted pulse generator delivered stimulation through electrodes over the lower spinal cord. This **epidural stimulation** reaches neural structures from outside the spinal cord itself. Adjusting the stimulated locations, pulse timing, and intensity helped recruit spinal pathways associated with particular leg movements, allowing the decoded cortical command to influence an output that the injury had made difficult to generate through the original descending route.

slides.title: Implanted devices exchange commands during movement
body: The brain–spine interface contained implanted cortical recording devices, a processing system, and an implanted spinal stimulator. Lorach and colleagues designed these components to exchange information during ongoing behavior. The cortical measurement was therefore not simply stored for later analysis; its decoded output changed the stimulation program while the participant attempted to stand or move the legs during use of the interface.

The processor estimated which movement was being attempted and how strongly to recruit the corresponding stimulation. This transformed a continuously changing neural measurement into a command with a physiological effect below the spinal injury. The source design demonstration shows how the recording, decoding, and stimulation components occupy different locations while operating as parts of the same functional system during movement.

Power, communication timing, and a stable signal affect whether the command arrives when the movement is needed. A delayed stimulation program could recruit a useful muscle group at the wrong part of the step. Coordinating the components allows the decoded leg intention to influence spinal activation in an order compatible with standing, initiating a step, and advancing the limb through the movement.

slides.title: Calibration pairs cortical patterns with spinal outputs
body: Lorach and colleagues calibrated the interface by recording cortical signals while the participant attempted selected leg movements. They identified signal features associated with those attempts and trained the decoder to distinguish them. This established a mapping from the recorded population activity to commands representing particular leg actions, rather than assuming that the same electrical pattern would mean the same movement for every individual.

The team separately tested spinal electrode configurations and stimulation parameters. Different settings recruited different combinations of muscles and movements. **Electromyography**, or **EMG**, measured electrical activity in the muscles, providing a physiological record of which outputs each program produced. This calibration paired a decoded cortical action with a stimulation pattern capable of helping generate a corresponding movement of the participant's leg.

The completed interface combined the two mappings during use. Cortical activity selected and modulated the spinal program, which changed muscle recruitment and limb motion. Measuring the resulting movement then revealed whether the command produced the intended action, allowing the system's neural input, stimulation output, and visible mechanical effect to be examined as distinct stages of the same attempted movement.

slides.title: Cortical commands help organize walking after injury
body: During interface use, the participant's cortical signals controlled spinal stimulation associated with leg movements. Lorach and colleagues measured changes in muscle activity and limb motion with the interface operating. The source demonstrations include standing and walking, showing how the decoded input and stimulation were used during recognizable actions rather than only during isolated contractions recorded while the participant remained stationary.

Walking requires the legs to alternate their supporting and advancing roles. The interface adjusted stimulation as the participant attempted successive movements, helping activate spinal pathways at the appropriate parts of that sequence. The resulting motion still depended on the participant's remaining nervous system, body mechanics, balance support, and sensory feedback from the moving limbs, rather than an external device moving the legs directly.

The participant also used the system for actions such as negotiating steps and changing the walking environment. These conditions require different combinations of joint movements from steady walking on a level surface. The demonstrations therefore examine whether cortical control can modulate stimulation as the intended action changes, rather than replaying one fixed sequence of stimulation pulses regardless of the participant's current movement attempt.

slides.title: Feedback closes the loop around neural control
body: An **open-loop controller** delivers a command without using the resulting outcome to adjust its next action. A fixed train of stimulation pulses can operate this way. In a **closed-loop system**, a measurement influences the command, and the consequences return through a feedback pathway that can change the following command during ongoing interaction with the body or the environment.

A brain–spine interface closes a loop through the participant. Neural activity changes stimulation, the legs move, and the participant receives visual and bodily sensory feedback about that movement. The participant can then adjust subsequent attempts. An automated controller can add another loop by using measured physiological or mechanical output to update the stimulation directly according to a specified control rule.

**Latency** is the delay between a measured event and the resulting command or response. Recording, data transmission, decoding, and stimulation each contribute part of this delay. A useful controller must deliver its output while the relevant state still persists, particularly when a short phase of movement requires one muscle group to be recruited before the next phase begins in the sequence.

slides.title: Rehabilitation changes performance without stimulation
body: Lorach and colleagues followed the participant during rehabilitation supported by the brain–spine interface. They also assessed movement without stimulation, separating immediate assistance from changes that persisted outside active interface use. After training, the participant could perform some movements and walk with crutches overground without stimulation, demonstrating an improvement in the measured unstimulated performance relative to the earlier assessment in the study.

The source comparisons include muscle recordings and walking measures across assessment periods. These measurements examine what the participant's remaining biological system could produce when the digital bridge was not supplying stimulation. Comparing device-on and device-off conditions answers different questions: one measures performance with current assistance, while the other describes retained function after the period of practice and rehabilitation supported by the interface.

The study did not show that the original injury had disappeared or that normal spinal anatomy had been restored. The observed improvement concerns motor function available through surviving biological pathways after training. Distinguishing this retained ability from the immediate effects of stimulation specifies what changed in the participant's performance without inventing a particular cellular repair process that was not directly measured in the clinical study.

slides.title: Cursor motion and selection require different commands
body: Pandarinath and colleagues used an intracortical BCI to support communication by people with paralysis. The participants controlled a cursor to choose letters on an on-screen keyboard. Cursor motion specified where to point, while a separate selection rule determined when a key was activated, allowing pointing and committing to a choice to be handled as different parts of the interface task.

One selection method detected a neural pattern associated with an intended click. Another used **dwell time**, selecting a target after the cursor remained within it for a specified interval. These approaches place different demands on the user: one requires producing a distinguishable selection pattern, while the other requires keeping the cursor inside the desired target long enough for selection to occur.

Keyboard layout also changes the movements required to produce a message. Nearby frequent letters can reduce cursor travel, while familiar layouts can make the intended target easier to find. The investigators compared several layouts and selection conditions, measuring the resulting text output rather than assuming that an accurate movement decoder alone determines how quickly a person can communicate through the complete cursor-based interface.

body: The brain–spine study included independent use of the interface by the participant. This required recording and stimulation to remain usable while the participant prepared the equipment and moved outside a tightly repeated laboratory sequence. The source demonstration shows operation of the actual system in this setting, preserving the distinction between an implanted device's technical design and the actions a person can carry out using it.

The cortical decoder continued to translate attempted movements into stimulation commands as the participant changed activities. Stable calibration reduced the need to rebuild that mapping for every brief use. The investigators reported that the system remained reliable over a year, including use at home, allowing the contribution of the interface to be examined across repeated sessions rather than a single successful demonstration during initial testing.

A change in terrain altered the mechanical demands even when the same general walking intention persisted. The participant's continuing sensory feedback and adjustments were therefore part of operating the interface across these different movement conditions in daily use.

slides.title: Neural control supports self-generated written messages
body: Pandarinath and colleagues tested **free-choice typing**, in which a participant composed an answer rather than copying a displayed sentence. The participant used recorded neural activity to move the cursor and select letters on the screen. The source recording follows this process through the production of an original response, showing the complete sequence from a question to a message created through the interface.

Visual feedback showed the cursor position, the selected letters, and the developing message. The participant could adjust the next movement or correct a mistake using this feedback. The decoder therefore operated within a continuing interaction between intention-related neural activity and the visible state of the keyboard, rather than generating an entire answer from one fixed measurement taken before typing began in the task.
